comparabilityWarning: Valid only against runs from this same machine and Node version, and only between runs whose round-trip calibration is similar. The same stack gave very different latencies on different occasions (see stability).

stability.reading: Not a stable measurement. Latency of the authenticated routes varied several-fold between runs of the same workload on the same machine, while event-loop numbers stayed close.
evidence: Trial at 20 req/s with 300 contacts (30 s): caller p50 39 ms, p95 87 ms.
Same stack, 10 req/s, 300 contacts (60 s): caller p50 226 ms, p95 1.8 s.
10 req/s, 5,000 contacts (60 s): caller p50 235 ms, p95 6.1 s.

First full run, 10 / 40 / 120 req/s, 5,000 contacts (evidence/load-run1-collapse-10-40-120.json): normal p50 819 ms, p95 2.8 s; peak (40 req/s) collapsed with caller p50 18.9 s, 16 % failed, 2,425 dropped iterations; spike 57 % failed. Loop delay p99 (median per profile) stayed at 40 to 55 ms in that run.
Seeding 5,000 contacts took 2.3, 9 and 7.6 minutes in three runs with identical code.
Host-to-Postgres `SELECT 1` round trips (100 sequential): p99 110.8 ms before the first profile and 43.9 ms after the spike, 2.5 to 4.3 ms in the other four calibrations (p50 1.2 to 3 ms throughout).
stability.likelyCause: Partly attributed (EL-011). Latency of an authenticated request tracks the host-to-container round-trip time times the roughly 12 sequential round trips each request makes: the same 20 req/s gave caller p95 66 ms when round trips were 2 to 3 ms and p95 11.8 s when they were 38 to 48 ms (evidence/auth-path-trace-after.json and auth-path-trace-before.json). Why the round trips were slow in some runs is NOT VERIFIED: a control with no application held 3 to 4 ms for five minutes (evidence/rtt-drift.json). A dedicated Linux host would answer it.

idle.reading: The resolution floor on Windows is about 15.5 ms (p50), so p99 under about 30 ms is quiet. The warn/critical windows counted here (5 / 1) come from the process settling after seeding.

peak.postgres: about 1.4 to 1.6 sessions on average 'idle in transaction' waiting on the client (the API) between statements; none long-running

spike.rate: 5 req/s, then 60 req/s for 40 s, then 5 req/s (achieved 19.2 req/s overall)

soak.reading: Ten minutes cannot show a leak that takes hours: heap +0.14 MB/min and RSS +2.7 MB/min over ten minutes are the shape of a stable process, not proof.

findings: The event loop was not what callers waited on. At 16.7 req/s callers saw p95 6.3 s while the API's loop delay p99 stayed near 33 ms (ELU median 0.29) and the unauthenticated /health control answered with p95 0.44 s. In the spike the loop delay p99 max was 93 ms while callers waited 12.7 s (median). The loop-delay alerts would not have paged in either profile; ApiCallerLatencyHigh (the probe) would have.

The wait is in the authenticated path's sequential round trips to Postgres and Redis (about 12 per request: 5 SQL statements and 7 Redis commands), not in the process; Postgres showed no long-running statements and its sessions showed 'idle in transaction' only for the round trip back to the API between a transaction's statements (EL-011). One redundant Redis lookup per request was removed; more are listed as EL-B17.

Client-side capacity on this machine: about 5 req/s is comfortable (p95 0.5 s), 17 req/s is degraded (p95 6.3 s, 1 % failed), 60 req/s collapses (12 % failed, 1,048 iterations dropped). These are properties of this laptop and this Docker setup, not of the product.
Soak at 5 req/s for ten minutes: no failures, memory flat.
